## A former Marine had an idea to help fellow veterans: AI helped him build it


November 9, 2026 · Written by Juan Montes


Years ago, Gary Crull spent an entire day helping a homeless veteran find the right hospital and get assistance.


That experience stayed with him. Crull, who served in the Marine Corps and the Army National Guard and now works as a management and program analyst at the[U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs](https://www.va.gov/) (VA), recently built[Battle Buddy](https://mybattlebuddy.ai/) , an AI agent that helps veterans, their families and caregivers make sense of federal, state and local benefits. The agent walks them through regulations and programs and often finds support people didn’t even know they could get.


“It was exhausting,” he remembers about his efforts trying to assist the fellow veteran. “If I had Battle Buddy during that time, I probably would have had more information right at the bat and probably had more direction.”


Back then, there was no such tool. Now Crull, who isn’t a professional developer, has built one himself. He’s a leading member of the[VA’s Citizen Developers](https://digital.va.gov/marketplace/user-guide/citizen-developer/) community: employees who aren’t professional programmers but use Microsoft Power Platform, the VA’s official citizen developer platform, to build low-code solutions to problems they see in their daily work.


[Some 17 million U.S. veterans](https://www.data.va.gov/dataset/Veteran-Population-by-State-FY2026/w6fb-7dn4/data_preview) can apply for hundreds of benefits and services, covering everything from disability compensation and healthcare to education, housing, employment and support for their families and survivors.


Crull knows the system from the inside. After deploying to Iraq, he served the public at the Veterans Benefits Administration, worked with veterans in the court system and gained further insight through the Veterans Experience Office.


“I had all the information at my fingertips because I’ve experienced it on both ends of the spectrum … my biggest saying is that Battle Buddy is made by veterans for veterans,” he says.


Crull built Battle Buddy with Microsoft[Copilot Studio](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/copilot/products/copilot-studio?msockid=036c6547c3cb6640028172b0c25267a6) , a graphical, low-code studio for building and managing AI-powered agents and workflows. As he explored Copilot Studio for another project, he quickly realized the potential to bring the agent concept to life.


## “I had all the information at my fingertips because I’ve experienced it on both ends of the spectrum … my biggest saying is that Battle Buddy is made by veterans for veterans“


*Gary Crull, management and program analyst at the U.S. Department of Veteran Affairs*


He built the knowledge base from a large collection of VA regulations, benefit information and other resources. He gathered thousands of discussions from veteran forums and compiled about 1,000 questions and answers, so the AI would learn both what veterans ask and how they ask it.


He later connected the agent to the federal regulations database, so changes could be reflected immediately, and to a VA system for location information. Crull trained Battle Buddy to understand the full veteran journey, from leaving military service to navigating hospital care, burial services and memorial agencies.


The agent could save veterans phone calls and trips to VA facilities and free up staff for more urgent cases. Some testers say they saved hours; others found information they had sought for more than a year.


## **From Marine to IT specialist**


Battle Buddy grew from two strands of Crull’s life: military service and technology. His military career ran from roughly 2002 to 2013. He began as a musician in the Marine Corps, then joined the Army National Guard and became an IT specialist.


During a 2010 deployment to Iraq, Crull built networks and taught Iraqis to use technology.


While working full time for the Indiana National Guard, he got early hands-on experience with Microsoft SharePoint, a secure platform for storing and sharing files, and later with Power Platform, Microsoft’s low-code platform for building apps and customized end-to-end business solutions.


In his current role at VA, Crull works on streamlining workflows across hospital systems and encourages colleagues to share what they know about technology. He created more than a few dozen apps to improve clinical operations, including the Leadership Rounding app, which addresses ineffective communication between employees and leadership in VA medical facilities.


“I love to learn … I’ve jumped from content to content, from topic to topic,” Crull says. “I’m passionate about learning new things and new technologies. I always want to push the limits.”


Crull developed Battle Buddy largely on his own, he says, but it now has VA support. The department provided Copilot Studio, funded licensing through its innovation program and authorized public field testing among groups of veterans.


“This technology can really help get me the answers to my veterans and their families sooner,” he points out. “When an employee can help a veteran and a veteran can get helped faster with this technology, what kind of price do you put on that?”


## **The outcome: testing in the field**


Battle Buddy is now in open field testing with veterans, Veteran Service Organizations (VSOs) and VA employees. It is available through links and QR codes, including inside[the VA Augusta Medical Center](https://www.va.gov/augusta-health-care/locations/augusta-va-medical-center-uptown/) in Georgia, although there is no timeline for a final release to the public.


Crull hopes the agent could save veterans time and help the VA use its resources more efficiently. An interaction with the agent takes 10 to 20 minutes, he says, compared to the hours or even days it can take a veteran to get all questions answered.


As Battle Buddy nears the end of testing, Crull is already working on a portal that connects organizations needing technical skills with employees who have them outside their formal roles.


“The biggest part of it is not only building these things but also passing that knowledge on to somebody who’s willing to learn,” he says.
